title: Java News Roundup: JDK 27-RC1, OpenJDK JEPs, Jakarta EE, BellSoft, Helidon, Micrometer, Tika 4.0
gist: A digest roundup covering JDK 27 entering release-candidate status (GA September 15, 2026, with nine finalized JEPs including default G1 GC and post-quantum TLS key exchange), two new JDK 28 JEPs (deprecating macOS/x64, a built-in JSON API), plus incremental releases across Jakarta EE, BellSoft Liberica JDK security patches, Helidon, Micrometer, and Apache Tika 4.0 which adds LLM-based OCR/inference modules.

insights.claim: Mark Reinhold, Chief Architect of the Java Platform Group at Oracle, formally declared JDK 27 has entered its first release candidate after Build 35 shipped with no unresolved P1 bugs, with general availability scheduled for September 15, 2026.
insights.speaker: Michael Redlich
insights.so_what: A hard release-date data point for enterprises planning JDK upgrade cycles and for vendors (Azul, BellSoft, Red Hat) that need to align downstream distribution releases to the September 15 GA.
insights.locator: As per the JDK 27 release schedule

insights.claim: JDK 27 will ship with JEP 523, Make G1 the Default Garbage Collector in All Environments, finalizing a shift that removes the prior environment-dependent default GC selection across all Java deployment contexts.
insights.speaker: Michael Redlich
insights.so_what: Teams running Java on non-standard environments (e.g., containers, embedded) that previously got a different default GC should validate G1 behavior before upgrading to JDK 27 to avoid unexpected pause-time or throughput regressions.
insights.locator: JEP 523: Make G1 the Default Garbage Collector in All Environments

insights.claim: JDK 27 finalizes JEP 527, Post-Quantum Hybrid Key Exchange for TLS 1.3, bringing post-quantum cryptography support into the standard Java TLS stack.
insights.speaker: Michael Redlich
insights.so_what: Signals the Java platform is now shipping production-grade post-quantum crypto by default, relevant for any regulated or security-conscious sector (finance, government) accelerating post-quantum migration timelines ahead of anticipated quantum-computing threats to classical encryption.
insights.locator: JEP 527: Post-Quantum Hybrid Key Exchange for TLS 1.3

insights.claim: JDK 27 also finalizes JEP 534, Compact Object Headers by Default, alongside advancing previews for Structured Concurrency (seventh preview), Primitive Types in Patterns/instanceof/switch (fifth preview), Lazy Constants (third preview), and the Vector API (twelfth incubator) -- a total of nine JEPs in the release.
insights.speaker: Michael Redlich
insights.so_what: Compact object headers by default is a memory-footprint win that reduces per-object overhead across all JVM workloads at scale -- material for infrastructure cost modeling on large heap-intensive Java fleets; the repeated multi-year preview cycles for Structured Concurrency and pattern matching show how slowly core language features stabilize in Java's governance process.
insights.locator: will include this final set of nine features

themes.theme: JDK 28 direction: platform pruning and a native JSON API

insights.claim: JEP 541, targeted for JDK 28, proposes deprecating the macOS/x64 port for removal because Apple no longer supports that architecture, following the same precedent as JEP 449's deprecation of the Windows 32-bit x86 port, explicitly to save on Java's own maintenance costs.
insights.speaker: Michael Redlich
insights.so_what: Confirms Apple's silicon transition is now driving upstream platform-support decisions in major language runtimes; any organization still running Java on Intel Macs needs a migration plan before this port is formally removed in a subsequent release.
insights.locator: JEP 541, Deprecate the macOS/x64 Port for Removal

insights.claim: JEP 540, targeted for JDK 28, adds a Simple JSON API (Incubator) implementing RFC 8259 directly into the JDK, removing the need for an external library like Jackson or Gson for basic JSON parsing/generation, and supersedes the withdrawn JEP 198 (Light-Weight JSON API).
insights.speaker: Michael Redlich
insights.so_what: A built-in JSON API reduces a common third-party dependency for simple use cases in the Java ecosystem, a small but recurring theme of the JDK absorbing functionality previously owned by the open-source library ecosystem (see also PEM encoding, JEP 542 below).

insights.claim: JEP 542, PEM Encodings of Cryptographic Objects, advanced from Candidate to Proposed to Target for JDK 28, finalizing a feature that went through three preview rounds across JDK 25-27, adding standard APIs to encode/decode PKCS #8 and X.509 objects to/from PEM text.
insights.speaker: Michael Redlich
insights.so_what: Another instance of the JDK internalizing cryptographic/interop plumbing that previously required third-party libraries, continuing a multi-release trend of native crypto/security feature expansion in the platform.
insights.locator: JEP 542, PEM Encodings of Cryptographic Objects

insights.claim: The Jakarta Agentic AI 1.0 specification, approved for creation in early November 2025, has delivered its first milestone (M1) release and a new project website, per Jakarta EE Developer Advocate Ivar Grimstad.
insights.speaker: Michael Redlich
insights.so_what: Enterprise Java is formally standardizing agentic-AI integration patterns (Jakarta Agentic AI spec) rather than leaving it to fragmented vendor frameworks -- worth tracking as a potential neutral interoperability layer for AI agents in large enterprise Java shops.

insights.claim: Jakarta EE 12 Core Profile remains on track for release in time for JakartaOne Livestream 2026, while the Web Profile and full Platform specifications are targeted for the first half of the following year.
insights.speaker: Michael Redlich
insights.so_what: Staggered release scheduling (Core Profile now, Web Profile/Platform later) signals Jakarta EE prioritizing a lightweight subset first -- relevant for enterprise Java teams sequencing platform upgrade plans.
insights.quote: The goal of releasing Jakarta EE 12 Core Profile in time for JakartaOne Livestream 2026 seems to be on track.
insights.locator: In his weekly Hashtag Jakarta EE blog

insights.claim: BellSoft released Critical Security Patch Updates for seven versions of its Liberica JDK distribution (26.0.2.1 through 6u513), concurrent with Oracle's August 2026 CPU, totaling 29 fixes and backports and eliminating 11 distinct issues across all releases.
insights.speaker: Michael Redlich
insights.so_what: Concrete patch-volume data point for security/compliance teams tracking Liberica JDK's patch cadence relative to Oracle's CPU cycle -- useful for vendor risk assessment of downstream OpenJDK distributions.
insights.locator: Concurrent with Oracle's Critical Security Patch Update

insights.claim: Apache Tika 4.0.0 reached GA with breaking changes -- document parsing now runs in its own forked process, configuration migrates from XML to JSON, and metadata keys are renamed under a tk: prefix -- alongside new inference and OCR modules supporting Claude, Gemini, OpenAI and Tesseract OCR.
insights.speaker: Michael Redlich
insights.so_what: A widely-used open-source document-parsing library now ships first-class integration with all three major LLM providers (Anthropic, Google, OpenAI) for inference/OCR, signaling that LLM-backed document understanding is becoming a default expectation in enterprise content-processing pipelines rather than a bespoke integration; the forked-process and config-format breaking changes mean any team on Tika 3.x needs a deliberate migration plan.

insights.claim: Helidon 4.5.3 tightens security defaults: participant callbacks in the Long Running Actions (LRA) component now require explicit authentication configuration (mp.lra.participant.url and a callback-auth secret), and JSON processing now caps nested object/array structures at 1000 levels.
insights.speaker: Michael Redlich
insights.so_what: The nested-structure cap is a hardening measure against resource-exhaustion/DoS attacks via deeply nested JSON payloads -- a pattern other JSON-processing library maintainers may want to adopt; Helidon users on LRA must update config before upgrading or callbacks will fail auth.

insights.claim: Micrometer Metrics 1.18.0-M1 removes its dependency on OpenTelemetry Protobuf Definitions in favor of the OpenTelemetry Metrics SDK and OTLP Exporter with shading, while Micrometer Tracing 1.8.0-M1 refactors its W3CPropagation class specifically to harden it against malicious injection, denial-of-service, and out-of-memory attacks.
insights.speaker: Michael Redlich
insights.so_what: The explicit security-hardening framing of the W3CPropagation refactor (injection/DoS/OOM) suggests trace-context propagation headers were an identified attack surface in distributed tracing infrastructure -- worth flagging to teams running Micrometer Tracing in adversarial-exposed services.
